Mark 1.audience: Mark wrote for readers who needed Jewish customs explained (Mark 7:3–4) and Aramaic words translated (Mark 5:41). Early tradition connects the Gospel with Peter's preaching and with Rome.

culture.title: Straightway
culture.text: The word translated "straightway" or "immediately" appears over forty times in Mark, giving the Gospel a rapid pace.

culture.title: The synagogue
culture.text: Synagogues were local meeting places for prayer and Scripture reading on the sabbath. Visiting teachers could be invited to speak.

culture.title: Peter's mother-in-law
culture.text: Extended families lived together in courtyard houses; Peter's household in Capernaum included his wife's mother.

Mark 2.audience: Mark records early conflicts with scribes and Pharisees in Capernaum over forgiveness, table fellowship, fasting, and the sabbath.

culture.title: Uncovering the roof
culture.text: Galilean roofs were made of beams covered with branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stairway. Friends dug through to lower the paralyzed man.

culture.title: Levi at the receipt of custom
culture.text: Capernaum lay on a trade route near a border, where tolls were collected on goods.

culture.title: Patching garments
culture.text: Unshrunk new cloth sewn onto an old garment shrinks when washed and tears the old cloth.

Mark 3.audience: Crowds come to Jesus from Galilee, Judea, Idumaea, beyond Jordan, and Tyre and Sidon (Mark 3:7–8). He appoints the twelve.

culture.title: Herodians
culture.text: The Herodians supported the rule of Herod's family under Rome. They joined the Pharisees against Jesus.

culture.title: Boanerges
culture.text: Jesus names James and John Boanerges, which Mark translates as "The sons of thunder."

culture.title: Binding the strong man
culture.text: A thief must first tie up the owner before plundering his house.

Mark 4.audience: Jesus teaches parables from a boat and then calms a storm on the Sea of Galilee.

culture.title: A candle under a bushel
culture.text: A bushel was a grain measure; a lamp covered by one would go out.

culture.title: Sudden storms
culture.text: The Sea of Galilee lies about 700 feet below sea level; winds rushing down from the surrounding hills can whip up sudden, violent storms.

culture.title: A Galilean boat
culture.text: In 1986 a first-century fishing boat about 27 feet long was found in the mud of the Sea of Galilee.

Mark 5.audience: Jesus heals a demon-possessed man in Gentile territory, a woman with a twelve-year illness, and raises Jairus' daughter.

culture.title: Living among the tombs
culture.text: Tombs cut in hillsides could shelter outcasts. Contact with the dead made a person ritually unclean.

culture.title: Legion
culture.text: A Roman legion had about 6,000 soldiers.

culture.title: Talitha cumi
culture.text: Mark preserves Jesus' Aramaic words, "Talitha cumi," and translates them: "Damsel, I say unto thee, arise."

Mark 6.audience: Jesus is rejected at Nazareth, sends out the twelve, and feeds five thousand. Mark tells of John the Baptist's death at Herod's banquet.

culture.title: The carpenter
culture.text: The word for carpenter (tekton) means a builder or craftsman in wood or stone. Nazareth was a small village near the growing city of Sepphoris.

culture.title: Herod's oath
culture.text: "Unto the half of my kingdom" echoes King Ahasuerus' words to Esther (Esther 5:3).

culture.title: Groups on the green grass
culture.text: Grass is green in Galilee in spring, near Passover (John 6:4). The crowd sits in groups of hundreds and fifties.

Mark 7.audience: Mark explains Jewish washing customs for readers unfamiliar with them (Mark 7:3–4) and notes that Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19).

culture.title: Washing pots and couches
culture.text: Pharisees washed cups, pots, brasen vessels, and tables according to purity rules. Stone vessels, which could not become impure, were common in Jewish homes.

culture.title: Corban
culture.text: Corban means ‘a gift’ dedicated to God. An ossuary lid found near Jerusalem bears the word as an inscription.

culture.title: Ephphatha
culture.text: Jesus says the Aramaic word "Ephphatha," which Mark translates "Be opened."

Mark 8.audience: After feeding four thousand, Jesus asks his disciples at Caesarea Philippi who he is, and Peter answers, "Thou art the Christ" (Mark 8:29).

culture.title: Leaven of the Pharisees
culture.text: Leaven—a lump of fermented dough—spread through the whole batch. It was a common image for hidden influence.

culture.title: Men as trees walking
culture.text: Only Mark records this healing at Bethsaida, which happens in two stages.

culture.title: Taking up the cross
culture.text: Condemned men carried their own crossbeam to the place of execution.

Mark 9.audience: Jesus is transfigured on a high mountain and teaches the disciples privately about his death and about humility.

culture.title: Elijah must first come
culture.text: Based on Malachi 4:5, the scribes taught that Elijah would return before the Messiah.

culture.title: Gehenna
culture.text: "Hell" here is Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, once a place of child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31).

culture.title: Salted with fire
culture.text: Every sacrifice was salted (Leviticus 2:13).

Mark 10.audience: Jesus travels toward Jerusalem through Judea and beyond the Jordan, teaching on divorce, wealth, and service, and heals blind Bartimaeus at Jericho.

culture.title: Women divorcing husbands
culture.text: Jewish practice allowed only a husband to divorce; under Roman law a wife could also divorce her husband.

culture.title: A ransom
culture.text: A ransom was a price paid to free a slave or captive.

culture.title: Begging by the road
culture.text: Blind beggars sat by busy roads, especially the pilgrim route near Jericho before the feasts.

Mark 11.audience: Jesus enters Jerusalem, curses a fig tree, and drives out traders from the temple courts.

culture.title: A colt never ridden
culture.text: An animal never used for ordinary work was considered fit for sacred purposes (Numbers 19:2).

culture.title: Figs out of season
culture.text: Fig trees put out small early fruit with their leaves in spring; a tree in full leaf without any promised a poor crop.

culture.title: The court of the Gentiles
culture.text: The outer temple court, open to Gentiles, was used for selling animals and changing money.

Mark 12.audience: In the temple, Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants and answers questions on taxes, resurrection, and the greatest commandment.

culture.title: A penny with Caesar's image
culture.text: The Roman denarius bore the emperor's portrait and title.

culture.title: Devouring widows' houses
culture.text: Scribes could manage estates for widows and might take advantage of them.

culture.title: Two mites
culture.text: A mite (lepton) was the smallest copper coin. Mark explains for his readers that two of them made a quadrans, a Roman coin.

Mark 13.audience: On the Mount of Olives, Jesus foretells the temple's destruction and warns his disciples to watch.

culture.title: Great buildings
culture.text: Herod's temple, rebuilt from about 20 BC, was one of the wonders of the Roman world.

culture.title: Councils and synagogues
culture.text: Local councils and synagogues could punish members with flogging (2 Corinthians 11:24).

culture.title: The watches of the night
culture.text: Mark names the four Roman watches: even, midnight, cockcrowing, and morning.

Mark 14.audience: Mark tells of the anointing at Bethany, the Last Supper, Gethsemane, the arrest, and Peter's denial.

culture.title: Spikenard
culture.text: Spikenard was a costly perfume from a plant grown in the Himalayas. Three hundred pence was nearly a year's wages.

culture.title: A man carrying a pitcher
culture.text: Carrying water jars was usually women's work, so a man doing it would be easy to spot.

culture.title: Abba
culture.text: Jesus prays "Abba, Father"—Abba is the Aramaic word for father used within a family.

Mark 15.audience: Jesus is tried by Pilate, crucified at Golgotha, and buried. Mark names Simon of Cyrene as "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21), apparently known to his readers.

culture.title: Golgotha
culture.text: Golgotha means "The place of a skull," a site just outside the city walls near a road.

culture.title: Wine mingled with myrrh
culture.text: Drugged wine was offered to dull the pain of crucifixion; Jesus refused it.

culture.title: The third hour
culture.text: The third hour was about 9 a.m.; darkness came at the sixth hour (noon) until the ninth (3 p.m.).

Mark 16.audience: Women come to anoint Jesus' body and find the tomb empty. The oldest surviving manuscripts end at Mark 16:8; verses 9–20 are found in most later manuscripts.

culture.title: Spices for the body
culture.text: Bodies were anointed with spices and wrapped in cloth for burial. The women waited until the sabbath was over.

culture.title: A very great stone
culture.text: Round rolling stones sealed some wealthy tombs and took several people to move.
